difficultyReason: Scientific/methodological argument about a drug trial. Correct answer confirms a load-bearing assumption (that the control group was truly comparable). Distractors include a plausible alternative explanation and a choice that strengthens a related but distinct conclusion.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical company conducted a six-month clinical trial in which patients with chronic migraines who took the new drug Veralox reported a 40 percent reduction in migraine frequency. Patients in the control group, who received a placebo, reported only a 10 percent reduction. The company concluded that Veralox is effective at reducing the frequency of chronic migraines.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some patients in the Veralox group reported mild side effects such as nausea during the first two weeks of the trial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patients in the Veralox group and those in the control group had similar average migraine frequencies before the trial began.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other drugs currently on the market have been shown to reduce migraine frequency by more than 40 percent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several patients who took Veralox also began practicing stress-reduction techniques during the trial period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The placebo effect is known to produce measurable reductions in self-reported pain in many clinical conditions.

explanations.correct: The argument's implicit assumption is that the treatment and control groups were comparable at baseline — otherwise the drug group's greater improvement might reflect pre-existing differences rather than the drug. Confirming that both groups had similar pre-trial migraine frequencies eliminates this confound and strengthens the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to the causal conclusion; mild side effects do not bear on whether the drug reduced migraine frequency.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms baseline comparability, ruling out the alternative that the drug group simply started with migraines more amenable to reduction.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — that other drugs are superior — while doing nothing to establish that Veralox itself is effective.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative explanation (stress-reduction techniques) for the drug group's improvement, thereby weakening rather than strengthening the argument.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant here; acknowledging the placebo effect is already accounted for by the control group design and does not further support the drug's efficacy.

difficultyReason: Economic policy argument where the correct answer rules out the most salient alternative explanation for observed data. Distractors include an irrelevant comparison and a choice that weakens by introducing a confounding trend.
stimulus: After the city of Harmon reduced its downtown parking fees by half, the number of shoppers visiting downtown stores increased by 30 percent over the following year. City planners attributed the increase in shoppers to the lower parking fees, arguing that the cost of parking had previously deterred people from shopping downtown.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city planners' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Downtown parking revenues declined significantly in the year following the fee reduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several other cities that reduced parking fees saw no corresponding increase in downtown shopping traffic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No new downtown stores opened, and no major downtown attractions were added during the year following the fee reduction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's overall retail sector grew by 35 percent in the same year, driven largely by increased consumer spending citywide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many shoppers who visited downtown stores during the year said they preferred shopping in open-air environments.

explanations.correct: The city planners assume that lower parking fees — not some other change downtown — caused the shopper increase. Ruling out new stores or attractions eliminates the most obvious alternative explanation, strengthening the causal attribution to the fee reduction.
explanations.A: Expected consequence of lower fees, not relevant to whether the fees caused more shoppers to come.
explanations.B: Weakens or introduces doubt by showing the proposed mechanism doesn't always hold elsewhere.
explanations.C: Correct. Rules out the competing explanation that new businesses or attractions, rather than lower fees, drew more shoppers.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative explanation — citywide consumer spending growth — that could account for the downtown increase without any role for parking fees, thereby weakening the argument.
explanations.E: Irrelevant; shoppers' preference for open-air settings has no bearing on whether parking costs drove the change.

difficultyReason: Environmental science argument with an implicit assumption about measurement reliability. Correct answer confirms the instrument's validity. Distractors include an opposite answer and a topically relevant but logically inert fact.
stimulus: Researchers monitoring a coastal wetland found that the concentration of a particular agricultural pesticide in the wetland water increased dramatically over the three years following the expansion of a nearby farm. They concluded that runoff from the expanded farm is the most likely source of the increased pesticide levels in the wetland.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pesticide detected in the wetland is the same compound used exclusively by the nearby expanded farm and not by any other farms or businesses in the region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pesticide concentrations in wetlands naturally fluctuate depending on seasonal rainfall patterns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The wetland supports several species of migratory birds that are known to be sensitive to pesticide exposure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expanded farm uses more water for irrigation than the farm did before its expansion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Environmental regulators had tested the wetland water five years prior and found no detectable levels of the pesticide.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that the expanded farm is the most likely source. Establishing that the detected pesticide is the same compound used exclusively by that farm and no other regional source directly eliminates competing sources, strongly supporting the causal attribution.
explanations.A: Correct. Rules out all other regional sources of that pesticide, making the nearby farm the only plausible origin.
explanations.B: Introduces an alternative explanation — natural fluctuation from rainfall — that could partially account for the increase, weakening rather than strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.C: Relevant to environmental impact but does nothing to establish the farm as the source of the pesticide.
explanations.D: Suggests higher runoff potential but does not establish that this runoff actually carries the specific pesticide to the wetland.
explanations.E: Confirms the pesticide appeared after the farm existed, consistent with many explanations; it does not narrow the source to the expanded farm specifically.

difficultyReason: Legal/policy argument with an analogical inference. Correct answer closes an analogical gap by confirming a key similarity. Distractors include an irrelevant statistic and a choice that strengthens a different conclusion.
stimulus: A law professor argues that mandatory minimum sentencing laws for nonviolent drug offenses should be repealed. She points to the state of Aldera, which repealed such laws a decade ago and subsequently saw a significant reduction in its prison overcrowding problem without any measurable increase in drug-related crime.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the law professor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prison overcrowding is widely considered one of the most pressing problems in the corrections systems of most states.

choices.label: B
choices.text: States with mandatory minimum sentencing laws for nonviolent drug offenses currently have significantly higher rates of prison overcrowding than Aldera had before its repeal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aldera's drug enforcement budget increased substantially in the years following its repeal of mandatory minimums.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The demographics, drug enforcement practices, and baseline incarceration rates of the states that currently have such laws are similar to those of Aldera before its repeal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many legal scholars believe that mandatory minimum sentences are inconsistent with the principle of proportional justice.

explanations.correct: The professor's argument relies on an analogy: what worked in Aldera will work in other states. The analogy's strength depends on the states being relevantly similar. Confirming that other states resemble Aldera in key respects closes the analogical gap and strengthens the inference.
explanations.A: Establishes that overcrowding is a serious problem broadly, but does not establish that Aldera's solution would work elsewhere.
explanations.B: Shows the problem is worse elsewhere — relevant context, but does not address whether Aldera's repeal strategy would transfer to other states.
explanations.C: Introduces a possible alternative explanation for Aldera's drug-crime stability post-repeal (increased enforcement), which actually weakens the argument that repeal alone produced the beneficial result.
explanations.D: Correct. Confirms the analogy holds by establishing that other states share the relevant features of Aldera prior to repeal.
explanations.E: A normative claim supporting repeal on grounds other than consequences — irrelevant to the empirical, consequentialist argument the professor makes.

difficultyReason: Technology/causal argument where the correct answer confirms an implicit mechanism. Distractors include a choice that appears mechanistic but actually supports a different conclusion, and an opposite answer.
stimulus: Engineers at a software company noticed that the incidence of critical software bugs reported by users increased sharply in the months after the company adopted a new automated code-review tool. They concluded that the automated tool was failing to catch bugs that the previous manual review process had caught.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the engineers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The automated code-review tool was used by several other companies before being adopted by this company.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The number of software updates released per month did not increase after the automated tool was adopted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The types of bugs reported by users after the tool was adopted were the same types that the manual review process had been specifically designed to catch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Automated code-review tools are generally faster at processing large codebases than manual review processes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: User reporting rates for software bugs are known to vary considerably depending on the visibility of a bug's effects.

explanations.correct: The engineers conclude the automated tool missed bugs the manual process would have caught. If the new bugs are precisely the types the manual process was designed to detect, it confirms that the manual process would have caught them — directly supporting the claim that the automated tool is the failure point.
explanations.A: Irrelevant; prior use by other companies neither confirms nor denies the tool's adequacy for this company's codebase.
explanations.B: Rules out the alternative that more frequent updates introduced more bugs, thereby strengthening by eliminating a competing explanation for the increase.
explanations.C: Correct. Confirms the mechanism — the new bugs are exactly those the manual process caught and the automated tool apparently misses.
explanations.D: Highlights a different advantage of automated tools; does nothing to address whether this particular tool catches the relevant bugs.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative explanation for the apparent increase in bugs — higher reporting rates — which weakens rather than strengthens the engineers' conclusion.

difficultyReason: Linguistics argument relying on a predictive inference. Correct answer confirms a load-bearing premise about the directionality of linguistic borrowing. Distractors include an accurate but irrelevant historical fact and a choice that strengthens only a peripheral claim.
stimulus: Linguists studying a remote island language discovered that roughly a third of its core vocabulary consists of words phonetically similar to words in a neighboring mainland language. Because the island was uninhabited until settlers arrived from the mainland approximately 800 years ago, the linguists concluded that these phonetically similar words were borrowed from the mainland language rather than the reverse.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Linguistic borrowing between island and mainland populations is a well-documented phenomenon in other parts of the world.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mainland language has remained relatively stable over the past 800 years, while the island language has changed substantially.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phonetically similar words in both languages predominantly refer to agricultural practices and tools that were established on the mainland long before the island was settled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The island language contains a large number of unique words with no counterparts in any known mainland language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several other island languages in the same region also share phonetic similarities with nearby mainland languages.

explanations.correct: The conclusion depends on the direction of borrowing: island borrowed from mainland, not vice versa. If the shared words refer to agricultural concepts well-established on the mainland before the island was settled, it is highly unlikely the mainland borrowed those terms from an island that did not yet exist as a settled community — directly supporting the borrowing direction the linguists claim.
explanations.A: Establishes that such borrowing occurs generally but does nothing to establish that borrowing in this case went from mainland to island rather than the other way.
explanations.B: Speaks to rates of linguistic change rather than direction of borrowing; does not address whether the similar words originated on the mainland.
explanations.C: Correct. Confirms that the shared vocabulary refers to mainland-established concepts, making it logically implausible that the mainland borrowed those words from a then-unsettled island.
explanations.D: Shows linguistic divergence but is irrelevant to whether the shared vocabulary was borrowed from the mainland.
explanations.E: Establishes a regional pattern consistent with borrowing but does not specify direction; similar to (A) in being accurate but not tightly supporting the directionality conclusion.

difficultyReason: History argument with an implicit assumption about evidence reliability. Correct answer validates the evidentiary basis. Distractors include a choice that introduces an alternative account and one that strengthens a different historical conclusion.
stimulus: Historians have long debated whether a great fire destroyed the ancient city of Veldara around 400 BCE or whether the city was abandoned gradually due to economic decline. A recent excavation uncovered a layer of ash and charred timber throughout the city's residential district at a depth consistent with the 400 BCE period. The excavation team concluded that a catastrophic fire, not gradual decline, ended Veldara's occupation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the excavation team's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ancient texts from a neighboring civilization describe a great conflagration that destroyed a major city in the region around 400 BCE.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several ancient cities contemporaneous with Veldara were abandoned as a result of prolonged economic pressures rather than sudden catastrophic events.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ash layer found in the residential district was also found beneath what was Veldara's commercial district, indicating the fire was city-wide.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Archaeological evidence of economic decline prior to 400 BCE has been found at several sites within the city.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Charred timber at ancient sites can sometimes result from controlled burning practices rather than accidental catastrophic fires.

explanations.correct: The conclusion requires that the ash layer resulted from a catastrophic fire and not gradual processes. An independent historical account from a neighboring civilization describing a great fire in the region at exactly this time corroborates the physical evidence, significantly strengthening the catastrophic-fire conclusion over the gradual-decline alternative.
explanations.A: Correct. Independent textual evidence corroborating a major fire in the region around 400 BCE strongly supports the physical evidence interpretation.
explanations.B: Supports the alternative (gradual decline) explanation by establishing that such outcomes were common, thereby weakening the team's conclusion.
explanations.C: Extends the geographic scope of the ash layer, consistent with a large fire, but this strengthens the conclusion more modestly than independent corroborating testimony; also it could suggest deliberate destruction rather than catastrophic accident. Still somewhat strengthening, but less directly than (A).
explanations.D: Supports the gradual-decline alternative by providing evidence consistent with economic trouble before 400 BCE, weakening the team's conclusion.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative explanation for charred timber (controlled burning), weakening the inference that the ash layer indicates a catastrophic fire.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy argument where the correct answer rules out an alternative that would undercut the normative conclusion. Distractors include an unwarranted comparison and a choice that is accurate but addresses only a peripheral premise.
stimulus: A bioethics committee argues that hospitals should be required to offer patients a standardized, one-page summary of any proposed surgical procedure in plain language before obtaining informed consent. The committee notes that patients who receive such summaries before other types of medical procedures demonstrate significantly better comprehension of risks and benefits than those who receive only verbal explanations.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the committee's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surgeons who provide verbal explanations of procedures often do so under significant time constraints that may reduce explanation quality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The complexity of risks involved in surgical procedures is not substantially greater than that of the other medical procedures for which written summaries have improved comprehension.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some hospitals already provide written procedure summaries voluntarily, and patient satisfaction scores at those hospitals are higher than average.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with lower health literacy levels are disproportionately likely to undergo surgical procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International medical associations in several countries have endorsed plain-language patient communication as a best practice.

explanations.correct: The committee's argument extends findings from 'other medical procedures' to surgical procedures specifically. The implicit assumption is that surgical procedures are sufficiently similar in complexity to those other procedures that the comprehension benefit would transfer. Confirming this similarity closes the analogical gap and strengthens the argument.
explanations.A: Supports the idea that verbal explanations are inadequate, lending some indirect support, but does not address the key inferential leap from non-surgical to surgical procedures.
explanations.B: Correct. Directly addresses the analogical gap — establishes that the complexity difference between surgical and other procedures is not so great as to undermine the transfer of the comprehension benefit.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — that voluntary adoption improves satisfaction — rather than establishing that mandated summaries would improve informed consent comprehension for surgical procedures.
explanations.D: Establishes a population need but does not confirm the proposed summaries would work for surgery specifically; accurate but does not bridge the analogical gap.
explanations.E: Appeals to authority, which may provide weak support, but international endorsement for general plain-language communication does not specifically establish the effectiveness of one-page surgical summaries.

difficultyReason: Arts/social science argument where the correct answer confirms a mechanism linking the observed correlation to the causal conclusion. Distractors include a choice that reverses cause and effect and one that introduces a confounding variable.
stimulus: A musicologist studying the relationship between early musical training and cognitive development found that children who began formal music lessons before age six scored notably higher on spatial reasoning tests at age ten than children who began lessons after age nine. She concluded that early musical training enhances the development of spatial reasoning abilities in children.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the musicologist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children who score highly on spatial reasoning tests at a young age are more likely than other children to be enrolled in music lessons by their parents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The children who began music lessons before age six did not differ significantly from the other children in household income, parental education, or access to enrichment activities other than music.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Learning to read musical notation requires children to mentally manipulate patterns and relationships in ways that directly exercise spatial reasoning pathways in the developing brain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spatial reasoning ability has been shown to correlate with performance in mathematics and engineering fields in adulthood.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some children who began music lessons before age six discontinued their lessons within the first year.

explanations.correct: The musicologist concludes that early music training causes enhanced spatial reasoning. The strongest support comes from identifying the mechanism by which this causal relationship operates. Showing that reading musical notation directly exercises spatial reasoning pathways in developing brains provides the mechanistic link that makes the causal conclusion most plausible.
explanations.A: Reverses the direction of causation — suggests higher spatial reasoning leads to music enrollment rather than vice versa — thereby weakening the argument by offering an alternative explanation for the correlation.
explanations.B: Rules out alternative confounding variables (socioeconomic factors), strengthening the causal attribution modestly, but does not confirm the mechanism by which training improves spatial reasoning.
explanations.C: Correct. Supplies the mechanism linking early music training to spatial reasoning improvement, directly confirming the causal pathway the musicologist posits.
explanations.D: Establishes downstream importance of spatial reasoning but says nothing about whether musical training caused the spatial reasoning scores observed in the study.
explanations.E: Introduces a complication — attrition — that might actually weaken the argument by suggesting the measured effect could be understated; irrelevant to whether the conclusion holds for those who continued.

difficultyReason: Policy/predictive argument where the correct answer bolsters a key load-bearing premise about behavioral response. Distractors include an irrelevant comparison and a choice that supports the conclusion by a different, weaker route.
stimulus: A transportation policy analyst argues that reducing highway speed limits from 70 mph to 60 mph on rural roads in Kentara Province will significantly decrease the annual number of fatal accidents. She bases this on the established relationship between vehicle speed and collision severity, and on data showing that most fatal rural accidents in Kentara occur at speeds above 65 mph.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies conducted in other provinces show that lowering speed limits typically reduces average travel speeds by an amount proportional to the limit reduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatal accident rates on rural roads in Kentara are higher than the national average.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kentara Province has adequate highway patrol resources to enforce a reduced speed limit on rural roads.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speed limits on rural roads in neighboring provinces have not been changed in the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The relationship between speed and collision severity has been studied primarily in urban environments rather than in rural settings.

explanations.correct: The analyst's argument requires that lowering the speed limit will actually cause drivers to reduce their speeds — otherwise the posted limit would have no effect on accident rates. Evidence from other provinces showing that reduced limits lead to proportionally lower average travel speeds confirms the behavioral mechanism the policy depends on, directly strengthening the argument.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms the key behavioral assumption: that lower limits translate into lower actual speeds, which in turn reduces fatal accidents via the established speed-severity relationship.
explanations.B: Establishes that the problem is serious but does nothing to confirm that the proposed speed limit reduction will solve it.
explanations.C: Addresses enforcement capacity, which is a relevant implementation concern, but the question is whether the policy will work if implemented, not whether it can be enforced — provides weaker, more indirect support than (A).
explanations.D: An irrelevant comparison; neighboring provinces' policies do not bear on whether Kentara's proposed change will reduce accidents.
explanations.E: Weakens the argument by suggesting the speed-severity relationship, a premise in the argument, may not transfer to the rural Kentara setting.
